stories.headline: Congo Ebola outbreak passes 4,000 deaths across seven provinces
stories.dek: Government data shows 8,300 confirmed cases, making this the biggest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in Congo's history.
paragraphs: Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak has now killed more than 4,000 people, according to government data released this week. The death toll reached 4,018 and confirmed cases rose to 8,300 across seven provinces. The new figures show the outbreak is still not under control.

This outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola. It began in Ituri province and has become the largest Ebola epidemic Congo has ever recorded, passing the 2018 to 2020 outbreak. More than 2,000 patients have recovered, but the virus has kept spreading into new areas.

Officials and the UN said in September that transmission appeared to be slowing in parts of Ituri. That has not stopped wider spread in eastern Congo, including North Kivu, or a new outbreak declaration in South Ubangi. It is still unclear when transmission will be brought down nationwide.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means Congo's health system and aid agencies still face a large, active Ebola emergency with risks of further spread.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Ebola is spreading globally now, or that every part of Congo faces the same level of risk.

cover.title: Congo Ebola outbreak passes 4,000 deaths in seven provinces
cover.standfirst: Democratic Republic of Congo said its Ebola outbreak has killed 4,018 people and infected 8,300 across seven provinces. The Bundibugyo strain has made this the country's deadliest Ebola epidemic on record. Officials say spread may be slowing in some areas, but the outbreak is still expanding elsewhere.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: Engrave eastern Democratic Republic of Congo as a dense, near-black landmass occupying the upper two-thirds, angled slightly, with province edges and forest texture fused into one heavy field. Carve a single pale river system through it from the northeast down toward the lower third; on first glance it reads as the Congo’s waterways, but the branching channel must unmistakably resolve into the split, looping seams of an Ebola filament advancing district by district. Keep the bottom third largely open cream, with only the river-path descending into it, so type can sit cleanly below.
art.note: Quiet, grave, monochrome with muted rust red accents.
art.second_beat: It first reads as Congo’s geography, then snaps into the realization that the country’s own river and movement corridors have become the virus’s shape — spread embedded in the map itself.

stories.headline: Wounded pilot helped stop cockpit attack on Flydubai flight
stories.dek: The captain said he forced open the cockpit door after being stabbed, letting passengers and off-duty pilots restrain the co-pilot.
paragraphs: A Flydubai captain injured in a cockpit attack has described how he helped stop it on Wednesday, in comments released from his Abu Dhabi hospital bed. He said he opened the cockpit door after being stabbed by the co-pilot, allowing others to enter and overpower him as the jet dropped sharply.

The Boeing 737 was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 182 people on board when it plunged about 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds over Saudi Arabia, according to flight-tracking data. The plane diverted to Tabuk and landed safely. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot, an Omani national.

Investigators in the UAE are still trying to establish motive, planning and whether the attack was linked to terrorism. Israeli officials said early signs point to radical Islamist indoctrination and a lone attacker, but that is not yet a final finding. The captain remains in hospital recovering from serious injuries.
stories.changes: Airlines and regulators will face fresh pressure to review cockpit access, crew screening and emergency procedures on passenger flights.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean commercial flying is broadly unsafe, or that every sharp descent points to an attack.

cover.title: Flydubai captain stopped cockpit attack after being stabbed mid-flight
cover.standfirst: A Flydubai Boeing 737 carrying 182 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv dropped about 14,000 feet in under 30 seconds on Wednesday after a co-pilot attacked the captain. The wounded captain said he opened the cockpit door so passengers and two off-duty pilots could restrain the attacker. UAE investigators are now examining motive and possible extremist links.

art.label: Flat character
art.concept: Show one Flydubai 737 in clean side cutaway, split once at the cockpit threshold into a left-right before/after. On the left: the sealed cockpit with two pilot figures and orderly passenger rows behind; on the right: the cockpit door forced open, the wounded captain collapsed just outside it, and a compressed surge of front-row passengers plus two distinct off-duty pilot figures pinning a single resisting co-pilot shape at the doorway. Keep the fuselage and seating geometry identical across both halves, but tip the nose slightly lower on the right and leave the lower third largely empty off-white for type.
art.note: Tense and controlled; cold cabin greys with harsh red accents.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a neat aircraft cutaway; a beat later you see it is the same plane split into the instant before and after the captain opens the cockpit, with the slight dip on the right turning the intervention into the thing that stopped the plunge.

stories.headline: Ara train crew worked route without required learning trips
stories.dek: Records show the loco pilot got one refresher trip, not two, before the Sikkim Mahananda Express derailment at Ara.
paragraphs: Railway records show the loco pilot in the September 7 Ara derailment was deployed on the Prayagraj-Patna route without the full route learning required by rules. This matters now because investigators have already blamed the crew for passing a red signal and reversing, and the records point to a second safety failure by managers.

Under railway norms, a loco pilot who has not worked a route for six months to two years must take two route-learning trips before regular duty. Records show this pilot last ran the route in December 2025, took one learning trip on July 1, 2026, and was then booked for regular runs from July 14.

The Railway Board had warned all zones on August 24 to stop exactly this kind of deployment and punish violations. Officials in Prayagraj have suspended the pilot, assistant pilot, crew controller and loco inspector. What remains unresolved is whether route-learning gaps directly contributed to the signal overshoot and who approved the booking.
stories.changes: It raises fresh doubt about whether railway safety rules are being enforced before crews are sent onto busy routes.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean every train on this route is unsafe or that route-learning gaps alone caused this derailment.

cover.title: Railway officials sent Ara train crew out without full route training
cover.standfirst: Railway records show the loco pilot in the September 7 Sikkim Mahananda Express derailment had not completed the two refresher trips required for the Prayagraj-Patna route. The Railway Board had warned all zones against this exact breach on August 24. Suspensions have followed, but the final chain of responsibility is still under review.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat signal-red ground, show a single railway signal post carrying not a signal head but a stiff, off-white route-learning duty card, cut like a blunt rectangle with ruled lines and punch marks but no readable text. Where the red lamp should be, and also where a second validation punch ought to be on the card, there is one raw torn hole straight through; a thick black marker arrow jabs at that absence, and the whole paper-signal leans slightly as if authority itself is based on a missing check. Keep the lower third clear and quiet for type: just the post descending into empty red.
art.note: Sharp, accusatory collage in railway red, dirty white and charcoal grey.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a stop signal; a beat later you see the 'red light' is actually the missing second route-learning punch, turning an absence in paperwork into the cause of the halted system.

stories.headline: Swiss glaciers lost nearly a fifth of their ice
stories.dek: Scientists say the recent loss in Switzerland is a sharp warning of faster warming in the Alps.
paragraphs: Scientists say Swiss glaciers have lost nearly a fifth of their volume in recent years. The finding was reported now as researchers warned that the pace of melt has become severe. One researcher called it a desperately needed warning sign for action on human-caused climate change.

Glaciers in the Swiss Alps store water, shape mountain landscapes and help mark long-term climate trends. When they shrink quickly, it points to warmer air, less lasting snow and hotter summers. Switzerland is closely watched because it has many well-measured glaciers in a densely studied mountain region.

The summary does not say which years were measured, which glaciers changed most or how this compares with earlier periods. It also does not say what Swiss officials will do next. The broader question is whether emissions cuts will come fast enough to slow further losses.
stories.changes: It adds to evidence that warming is changing mountain water, landscapes and winter conditions faster than many people expect.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean all Alpine ice will disappear at once or that one study alone settles every local forecast.

cover.title: Scientists say Swiss glaciers lost nearly a fifth of ice
cover.standfirst: Scientists say glaciers in Switzerland have lost nearly 20 percent of their volume in recent years. The sharp decline in the Alps is a warning about human-driven warming. Researchers are using the finding to press for faster cuts in greenhouse gas emissions.

art.label: Decorative flat
art.concept: Show one unmistakably Swiss Alpine mountain face split into two adjacent states of the same glacier, using the exact same ridge, fir bands, and moraine contours so the subtraction is undeniable. On the left, the glacier sits broad and low in the valley; on the right, that same ice body has retreated sharply upslope, leaving a raw brown lower basin and a few thin blue melt streams where the missing ice used to be. Keep the lower third mostly quiet with simple valley tone and sparse detail, and place one tiny red-jacketed climber on the same traverse line crossing both halves for scale and continuity.
art.note: Cool alpine blues and whites against raw brown rock; quiet, stark, unsentimental.
art.second_beat: First you read a clean before/after comparison; second you realise the mountain profile is identical, so the missing fifth lands as a physical removal, not an abstract climate statistic.

stories.headline: World food prices rose in September to a near four-year high
stories.dek: The UN food price index reached 136.0 points in September, up from a revised 134.0 in August.
paragraphs: World food prices rose again in September, reaching their highest level in nearly four years, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. The FAO Food Price Index averaged 136.0 points, up from a revised 134.0 in August. The new reading shows broad pressure in global food markets this month.

The FAO index tracks monthly changes in international prices for a basket of widely traded food commodities. It is used as a global benchmark for staples bought and sold across borders. A higher reading does not mean every shopper pays the same amount, but it signals stronger import costs and market strain.

The summary does not say which foods drove the increase most or whether the rise will last into October. It also does not show how quickly higher global prices will reach local shops. National harvests, exchange rates, subsidies and transport costs will still shape what families actually pay.
stories.changes: This raises the risk of higher grocery bills, especially in countries that import a large share of their food.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean every food item will rise at once or that shortages are now certain.

cover.title: UN says world food prices reached near four-year high
cover.standfirst: The UN food price index averaged 136.0 points in September, up from a revised 134.0 in August. The reading is the highest in nearly four years and points to renewed pressure in global food trade. What happens next depends on which commodities rose and how local markets pass costs on.

art.label: Drawn chart
art.concept: On an otherwise empty cover, make a clean rising bar chart out of a row of supermarket receipts, each one hanging straight down and slightly taller than the last. The final receipt, in the accent colour, is actively feeding out of a plain checkout slot cropped into the top edge, its paper still curling as it drops and extending lowest into the frame; keep the lower third largely open apart from the bottoms of the receipts so type can sit across it.
art.note: Calm, factual mood; warm grain colors with sharp red for the rise.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a rising chart; a beat later you realise the bars are till receipts, turning a global food-price index into the household bill it becomes.

stories.headline: US presses Europe to tap diesel reserves amid export ban threat
stories.dek: Trump says Europe should release diesel stocks as Washington weighs curbing exports to cut US fuel prices before November.
paragraphs: Donald Trump said he may ask European countries to release diesel from emergency reserves while he considers banning US diesel exports. He wants lower fuel prices at home before the November elections. The threat has alarmed European governments because US diesel is a key part of their supply.

Diesel markets are already tight. War around Iran has disrupted oil and fuel flows, and Europe has bought more diesel from the US since Russian supplies fell away. The UK imports more than half its diesel, with about 31% of those imports coming from the US.

No ban has been announced, and officials are still talking. European governments are discussing a coordinated response and possible reserve releases if needed. The main unknown is whether Trump follows through, and how far prices rise outside the US if American exports are cut.
stories.changes: Diesel users in Europe, including drivers, hauliers and farmers, may face higher prices soon if US exports are restricted.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean an immediate diesel shortage, and governments still say supply systems and emergency stocks remain in place.

cover.title: US asks Europe to use diesel reserves as export ban looms
cover.standfirst: Donald Trump said European countries should prepare to release diesel stocks while his administration weighs restricting US diesel exports before the November elections. The UK gets 31% of its diesel imports from the US, and European officials are now discussing a joint response and possible reserve use.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Draw the Atlantic crossing as a single thick diesel hose snaking from a simplified US East Coast at left toward the UK and northwest Europe at right. Mid-ocean, the hose is being pinched shut by a hooked hand/finger shape entering from the US side, so the route reads first as a map line and then as a deliberately constricted fuel line; on the Europe side of the pinch, two or three tiny tanker silhouettes bunch up uselessly near the coast. Keep the lower third largely open sea for type, and use two hard Riso colours so the pinched point and backed-up flow carry the whole image.
art.note: Tense and public-facing, with muted red, navy and fuel-grey.
art.second_beat: First it reads as an Atlantic trade route; a beat later you see it is a fuel hose being deliberately squeezed shut by Washington before Europe can draw supply.

stories.headline: French high school protests shut about 400 schools nationwide
stories.dek: Students blocked gates, lit fires and clashed with police over long hours, poor conditions and repeated staff absences.
paragraphs: French high school protests spread across the country on Friday, forcing the closure of about 400 schools. Students blocked entrances, lit fires outside some campuses and faced police in several places. The unrest grew after days of action over long school hours, poor classroom conditions and missing staff.

The movement began last week around Paris and quickly reached other regions. It involves pupils at lycees, the final years of secondary school in France. Protesters say some classrooms are overheated and schools are understaffed. The government says these complaints are real but calls the street violence unacceptable.

It is still unclear how long the closures will last or whether ministers will offer new measures. More protests could disrupt classes again next week. The main unresolved issue is whether officials can answer student complaints without wider clashes between teenagers and police outside school gates.
stories.changes: If you have family or school ties in France, classes, travel around campuses and local policing may be disrupted in the short term.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean France's whole school system has shut down or that every protest has turned violent.

cover.title: French student protests force closure of about 400 high schools
cover.standfirst: French high school students blocked gates and lit fires outside some campuses on Friday, as protests over long hours, poor conditions and staff absences spread nationwide. About 400 schools closed. The government accepts some complaints but says the violence must stop.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a pale blue seamless, place a real section of French lycée gate in the centre, its vertical bars twisted into a tight knot so the entrance has physically tied itself shut. Just beyond it, near the upper right, leave a single school exercise book lying flat with one corner and page edges lightly scorched; keep the lower third almost empty except for the gate’s quiet shadow so type can sit cleanly. Shoot it deadpan and frontal, with enough detail in the metalwork that it reads unmistakably as a school gate rather than generic fencing.
art.note: Tense public-street mood; red, navy, black and pale concrete tones.
art.second_beat: First read: the gate is impossibly knotted shut; second beat: the singed French school notebook turns a surreal closure into this week’s lycée blockades and clashes.

stories.headline: SpaceX Crew 13 reaches space station for six-month mission
stories.dek: Four astronauts from more than one country launched Thursday morning and began docking at the International Space Station that night.
paragraphs: SpaceX Crew 13 is arriving at the International Space Station after launching Thursday morning. The four-person crew began docking Thursday night. They are starting a mission expected to last about six months, adding fresh staff to the orbiting laboratory for research and station work.

The International Space Station is a permanently crewed lab in low Earth orbit. Crews rotate in and out on scheduled missions that usually last months. SpaceX carries many of those crews for NASA and its partners, bringing astronauts, supplies, and replacement personnel to keep experiments running.

The immediate unknown is whether docking and hatch opening finish on schedule and without technical trouble. The summary does not say which countries the four crew members represent or which experiments they will lead. More details are likely after arrival, safety checks, and the handover with the current crew.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this keeps the station staffed and its science program running on the usual rotation.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean space travel has become routine for the public or that daily life on Earth changes overnight.

cover.title: Four astronauts dock at the International Space Station
cover.standfirst: A four-person international crew launched on Thursday morning aboard SpaceX Crew 13 and began docking with the International Space Station that night. They are due to spend about six months aboard the orbiting lab, taking over research and station duties from the current crew.

art.label: Made object
art.concept: Build a simplified handmade ISS from white card modules, pipe-cleaner truss and two unmistakable rectangular solar-panel wings, cropped on the right so it feels large and already in place. From the left, a white clay Crew Dragon is arriving nose-first — but its body is subtly transformed into a chunky six-page flip-desk-calendar form: a stack of thick white pages with a visible page-block edge and curved stand-like back, while still keeping the Dragon’s black window band and docking nose so it reads first as spacecraft, then as a six-month stint made physical. Hold it just before contact, with the lower third left mostly plain deep blue for type.
art.note: Calm, precise, dark space blues with bright white hardware and warm window light.
art.second_beat: First you see a Dragon docking with the ISS; a beat later you realize the capsule is also the crew’s six-month rotation, turning the mission duration itself into the thing SpaceX delivers.

stories.headline: Wilson scores 36 as Aces end Fever season in Game 3
stories.dek: Las Vegas beat Indiana 94-83 after Caitlin Clark returned with a bloodied mouth from a late no-call collision.
paragraphs: A’ja Wilson scored 36 points and took 10 rebounds as the Las Vegas Aces beat the Indiana Fever 94-83 on Thursday night in the deciding first-round game. The defending champions needed their star at her best after Indiana cut the lead to two points twice in the fourth quarter.

Las Vegas, the No 3 seed, have now ended Indiana’s season two years running. Caitlin Clark scored 18 points after 11 in the first quarter, while Kelsey Mitchell had 23 and Aliyah Boston added 19 points and 10 rebounds. Chelsea Gray scored 23 for the Aces and Jackie Young added 18.

The game stayed tense to the end. Clark briefly left after an accidental elbow from Jewell Loyd appeared to knock out a tooth and left her bleeding, but no foul was called and she returned. Las Vegas now wait to learn whether they face Golden State or Dallas next.
stories.changes: For fans, the result means Las Vegas stay alive in the title race and Indiana's season is over.
stories.unchanged: One bruising playoff game does not settle every argument about Clark, officiating or the balance of power in the WNBA.

cover.title: Las Vegas Aces beat Indiana Fever as A'ja Wilson scores 36
cover.standfirst: The Aces won 94-83 in Las Vegas on Thursday to take the deciding first-round Game 3 and end Indiana's season. Wilson added 10 rebounds, while Caitlin Clark finished with 18 points and returned after leaving the court with a bloodied mouth late in the game.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Paint a backboard, rim and white net from a slight low angle inside Gainbridge Fieldhouse, with the arena reduced to a few muted bands so the lower third stays open and quiet for type. Instead of a normal ball, the Indiana Fever’s unmistakable navy-and-gold sunburst basketball mark is being dragged halfway through the net, stretched and cinched so it reads as the whole season being forced out in one motion; the cords should bite into it hard enough to feel trapped, not scored. Keep everything else out — no players, no extra props, no text-dependent details — just the hoop, the net, and the Fever identity caught in the act of ending.
art.note: Tense and kinetic, with hard arena light and sharp team colors.
art.second_beat: First read: a made basket; second beat: it isn’t a ball at all but the Fever itself being squeezed through the net, turning a score into a season-ending elimination.

stories.headline: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties after mutual accusations
stories.dek: The two Horn of Africa neighbours accused each other of feeding internal conflicts and severed formal relations.
paragraphs: Ethiopia and Eritrea have broken diplomatic ties after each government accused the other of stirring unrest inside its borders. The break appears to follow a new rise in tension between the two neighbours. It cuts official contact at a time when the region is already fragile.

The two countries share a long, troubled history of war, border disputes and short-lived rapprochement. Their relationship matters far beyond the frontier because instability can spread across the Horn of Africa. A break in ties can affect border management, trade links, security cooperation and movement between the states.

It is not yet clear what exact steps each side has taken, such as closing embassies, expelling diplomats or restricting crossings. It is also unclear whether outside mediators will try to lower tensions soon. The main risk now is that hostile language could harden into wider political or military confrontation.
stories.changes: For ordinary people in the region, travel, trade and contact across the Ethiopia-Eritrea border may become harder and less predictable.
stories.unchanged: This does not by itself mean a new war has started, and many daily services inside each country will continue as normal for now.

cover.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever ties after conflict accusations
cover.standfirst: Ethiopia and Eritrea have broken diplomatic ties after accusing each other of fuelling internal conflicts. The split deepens tension between two neighbours with a long record of war and border disputes. It is not yet clear whether embassies will close or whether mediators will step in.

art.label: Newsprint collage
art.concept: A heavy old telephone handset, built from blunt newsprint collage shapes, is dropping diagonally out of the upper half of the cover as if just let go. Its cord is not a cord but a taut barbed-wire border fence running horizontally across the page; at the point of strain several barbs and wire twists are snapping free, so the line meant to carry speech has hardened into a frontier. Keep the lower third largely open and quiet for type, with the break and falling motion happening above it against one flat ground.
art.note: Tense, spare, dusty palette with faded reds, ochres and hard shadows.
art.second_beat: First you see a call cut off; a beat later you realise the phone line itself has become the border, so diplomacy has turned into obstruction.
